suggestions.rationale: Erectile dysfunction and depression show a clinically important bidirectional association at the population level, but the available observational evidence does not establish the causal direction in an individual patient. A 49-publication systematic review and meta-analysis found increased odds of depression among men with erectile dysfunction and increased odds of erectile dysfunction among men with depression. This relationship should therefore be evaluated with symptom chronology, functional impact, treatment history, medication effects, vascular/endocrine contributors, and mental-health assessment rather than being presented as automatic secondary causation.
evidenceGaps: Mental-health evaluation confirming depressive disorder and onset
Records describing distress, relationship impact, function, and quality of life when present
Medication, vascular, endocrine, neurologic, and other competing-cause review
Clinician assessment of the likely direction and contributors in the individual case

sourceReferences.citation: Liu et al., The Association Between Erectile Dysfunction and Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, J Sex Med. 2018;15(8):1073-1082. PMID 29960891
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 publications found a bidirectional association between erectile dysfunction and depression; the authors note that observational evidence cannot determine causality. Supports conservative association/pathway research, not an automatic individual nexus.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 29960891; 49 publications; ED-to-depression analysis included 192,455 participants and depression-to-ED analysis included 14,008; discussion notes observational data cannot determine causality
